hints: Think about the journey of one red blood cell - how many times does it go back to the heart before it has visited both the lungs and the rest of the body?
walkthrough:
Picture Two Loops Meeting at the Heart**
Imagine the heart in the middle with two separate loops coming out of it. One short loop goes to the lungs and back, and one long loop goes to the rest of the body and back.

Count the Visits to the Heart**
For blood to complete a full tour it must go heart to lungs to heart, then heart to body to heart. That is two separate passes through the heart, which is why it is called double. The lung loop is the pulmonary circulation and the body loop is the systemic circulation.
Final answer: Blood passes through the heart twice for each complete circuit of the body, once through the pulmonary circulation and once through the systemic circulation.

hints: Look closely at Fig. 3.1 - what do those thin white string-like threads connect between the valve flap at the top and the muscle below?
Think about what happens when the ventricle squeezes hard - what would stop the floppy AV valve from being pushed backwards up into the atrium?
Link the name of these cords to their anchoring points - papillary muscle to AV valve - and to keeping blood flow one-way.
walkthrough:
Recognise the Heart Strings**
Those white threads are the chordae tendineae, sometimes called tendinous cords or heart strings. They run from the cusps of the atrioventricular valve (bicuspid or tricuspid) down to the papillary muscles in the ventricle wall.

Hold the Valve Against High Pressure**
When the ventricles contract in ventricular systole, blood pressure rises sharply. Without anchoring, the AV valve flaps would be forced inside-out up into the atrium. The papillary muscles contract too, pulling on the chordae tendineae so they become taut and hold the valve firmly shut in position.

Keep Blood Moving One Way**
By preventing the valve from inverting, the chordae tendineae prevent backflow into the atrium. Blood can therefore only leave the ventricle forward into the aorta or pulmonary artery, maintaining one-way flow through the heart.

Final answer: Structure A: chordae tendineae (tendinous cords). They connect the atrioventricular valve to papillary muscle and become taut during ventricular systole to hold the valve in position and prevent inversion, preventing backflow of blood into the atrium and ensuring one-way flow.

hints: Compare the two rows in Table 3.1 carefully - is the target inside the bacterium the same for gentamicin and penicillin G?
Think in terms of chance - if a bacterium happens to gain resistance to one drug, what kills it, and how likely is it to gain resistance to both drugs at once?
walkthrough:
Use Two Different Weapons**
Table 3.1 shows gentamicin binds permanently to bacterial ribosomes to stop protein synthesis, while penicillin G inhibits an enzyme for cell wall synthesis. Because they attack different targets, resistance to one does not give resistance to the other.

Make Double Resistance Almost Impossible**
If a bacterium mutates to resist penicillin G, gentamicin will still kill it, and vice versa. To survive both drugs a single bacterium would need two separate resistance mutations in different genes at the same time, which has an extremely low probability. That is why the combination ensures all bacteria are killed and resistance is less likely to develop.

Final answer: Gentamicin and penicillin G have different sites of action (ribosomes and cell wall synthesis enzyme). A bacterium resistant to one is still susceptible to / killed by the other, and the probability of two resistance mutations occurring in the same bacterium is very small.

hints: Start from the source of all new variation in bacteria - what random change in DNA could alter the gentamicin target shown in Table 3.1?
Think about what happens if the antibiotic course is stopped early - which bacteria survive and what do they do next?
Connect survival to inheritance - how does the resistance allele spread through the population and become common when gentamicin is used again?
walkthrough:
Mutation Creates the Resistant Variant**
Resistance starts with a random mutation in bacterial DNA, for example in the gene coding for the ribosomal protein. This can change ribosome structure so gentamicin can no longer bind permanently, or produce an enzyme that breaks down gentamicin. Mutations are not caused by the antibiotic, they already exist by chance.

Incomplete Treatment Lets Survivors Multiply**
If the course is not completed, not all bacteria are destroyed. The less susceptible bacteria survive while susceptible ones are killed. Survivors then replicate rapidly by binary fission, and more replication gives more chances for further mutation.

Selection and Spread Increase Resistance**
The resistance allele is inherited by daughter cells in vertical transmission and can also pass between bacteria by horizontal transfer such as conjugation or transformation. When gentamicin is next prescribed, it acts as a selection pressure: resistant bacteria are selected for and susceptible bacteria are selected against, so the frequency of the resistance allele in the population rises.

Final answer: Random mutation in a gene produces a resistance allele, e.g. altered ribosome structure so gentamicin cannot bind. If the antibiotic course is not completed, less susceptible bacteria survive and replicate. The resistance allele is passed on by vertical transmission and horizontal transfer (conjugation/transformation) and is selected for when gentamicin is present as selection pressure, increasing its frequency.
